title: Tooth Pain That Won't Go Away: Could It Be the Nerve?
metaTitle: Tooth Pain That Won't Go Away: Is It the Nerve?
metaDescription: Tooth pain that won't go away may mean the nerve is involved. Learn the warning patterns, other possible causes, and why acting early helps.
excerpt: Why persistent tooth pain can signal nerve involvement, how dentists tell it apart from other causes, and why early care matters.
heroImageAlt: A person resting a hand on their jaw, bothered by a toothache that will not ease.
bodyHtml:
If a tooth hurts and the pain simply will not go away, the nerve inside the tooth — part of the soft tissue called the pulp — may be inflamed or infected. Persistent toothache is one of the more common reasons the pulp is involved, although not the only one. The key point is reassuring and practical: ongoing pain is your body's signal to have the tooth checked, and acting early often makes any needed treatment simpler.

What the pulp does

Deep inside each tooth is the pulp, which contains nerves and blood vessels. When decay, a crack, a deep filling, or an injury lets bacteria reach this tissue, it can become inflamed or infected. Because the pulp is sealed inside the tooth, that inflammation has nowhere to go, which is why the resulting pain can be persistent and, at times, intense.

When ongoing pain suggests the nerve

Several patterns make dentists suspect the pulp rather than a passing irritation:

  • Pain that lingers long after hot or cold, instead of fading in a second or two.
  • Throbbing or spontaneous pain that arrives without a trigger.
  • Pain that disturbs your sleep or worsens when you lie down.
  • Tenderness when biting on a specific tooth.

These are not a diagnosis on their own, but together they raise the likelihood that the nerve is affected and that the tooth should be examined.

Other causes worth ruling out

Not all lasting tooth pain comes from the pulp. Gum disease, an exposed root surface, a cracked filling, sinus pressure, or grinding can all cause discomfort. This is exactly why a professional assessment matters: a dentist can distinguish pulpal pain from these other sources using an examination and X-rays, rather than you having to guess.

Why acting early helps

When the pulp is inflamed but still healthy enough, the situation is sometimes more manageable. If infection sets in and the pulp dies, treatment such as a root canal is often needed to save the tooth, and an untreated infection can spread. Seeking care early does not guarantee any particular outcome, but it generally keeps your options broader and your treatment more straightforward.

What a visit involves

A dentist will ask about your pain, test how the tooth responds to temperature and pressure, and take radiographs to look at the root and surrounding bone. From there, they can explain whether the nerve is involved and what the sensible next steps are, whether that is monitoring, a filling, a root canal, or a referral.

Keeping track of your symptoms

Before your appointment, it helps to notice a few details about the pain, because they guide the diagnosis. Is it triggered by hot, cold, or biting, or does it arrive on its own? How long does it last once it starts? Does it keep you awake, or ease when you take pain relief? Is it clearly one tooth, or hard to pinpoint? Jotting down answers to these questions gives your dentist a clearer picture and can save time during the examination. None of this replaces a professional assessment, but it turns a vague "my tooth hurts" into useful information, and it often helps you feel more in control of a situation that can be unsettling while you wait to be seen.

Should I just take painkillers and wait?

Pain relief may help temporarily, but it does not treat the cause. If pain keeps returning, have the tooth assessed rather than relying on medication alone.

Is sudden severe pain an emergency?

Severe pain, especially with swelling or fever, should be seen promptly. Many clinics set aside time for urgent dental concerns.

Can nerve pain go away by itself?

Pain can sometimes ease if the nerve dies, but that does not mean the problem is solved — infection can still develop. Easing pain is not the same as healing.

If a toothache has outstayed its welcome, it is worth having it looked at. You can learn more about the team at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham and how they handle urgent concerns on the clinic's dental emergencies page.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
